related_questions.question: What is the first line treatment for CMV retinitis?
related_questions.snippet: First-line treatment for both HIV-positive and HIV-negative patients with CMV retinitis is typically induction therapy with either intravenous (IV) ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir (31–33), followed by maintenance therapy (12,33,34).

related_questions.question: Does CMV retinitis resolve?
related_questions.snippet: Although treatments are available, you cannot get back vision lost because of CMV retinitis. Even with treatment, the disease may still progress. Recurrence of CMV retinitis is common, so regular checkups with an ophthalmologist are important.

related_questions.question: What is the most appropriate treatment of peripheral CMV retinitis?
related_questions.snippet: Intravitreal ganciclovir, foscarnet, or cidofovir can be considered for short-term management. Other options for therapy are oral leflunomide and oral letermovir. These therapies are using much less often but have been effective in patients that are experiencing side effects of other medications.

related_questions.question: What is the treatment of choice for CMV?
related_questions.snippet: The drug of choice for the treatment of CMV disease is intravenous ganciclovir, although valganciclovir may be used for nonsevere CMV treatment in selected cases. Ganciclovir is a nucleoside analogue that inhibits DNA synthesis in the same manner as acyclovir.

text_blocks.snippet: Treatment for CMV retinitis, an eye infection caused by the cytomegalovirus, focuses on stopping the virus from replicating and preserving or improving vision. This is typically achieved through antiviral medications administered in different ways, alongside addressing the underlying systemic condition.
snippet_highlighted_words: antiviral medications administered in different ways, alongside addressing the underlying systemic condition

list.snippet: Ganciclovir: Often used intravenously or as a sustained-release implant in the eye (Vitrasert).
Valganciclovir: An oral medication that is a prodrug of ganciclovir, making it easier to administer.
Foscarnet: Another antiviral medication, sometimes used when other treatments are not effective or tolerated.
Cidofovir: Can be administered intravenously or directly into the eye (intravitreal).
Maribavir: A newer oral medication approved for refractory or resistant CMV infections.
Intravitreal Injections: Injections of ganciclovir or foscarnet directly into the eye can provide high drug concentrations locally.
Vitrasert Implant: A sustained-release implant that releases ganciclovir into the eye over time.
Intravenous (IV) Antivirals: Medications like ganciclovir or foscarnet are administered through an IV line.
Oral Antivirals: Valganciclovir is an example of an oral antiviral that can be used for maintenance therapy.
For patients with HIV/AIDS, antiretroviral therapy (ART) is crucial for controlling the CMV infection and preventing recurrence.
Treatment of other underlying conditions like leukemia may also be necessary.

list.title: Induction:
list.snippet: A more intensive phase of treatment, often involving higher doses of antivirals, to rapidly control the infection.

list.title: Maintenance:
list.snippet: A longer-term phase of treatment, often with lower doses of antivirals, to prevent recurrence of the infection.
Regular eye exams are essential to monitor the progression of the retinitis and response to treatment.
Blood work is also monitored during treatment to assess for any side effects.
CMV retinitis is a serious condition that can lead to vision loss if not treated promptly and effectively.
Treatment often requires a combination of approaches and may need to be continued long-term.
Early diagnosis and prompt treatment are crucial for maximizing the chances of preserving vision.
